sources.text:
A scheduler chooses which ready job receives the processor. Turnaround time equals completion time minus arrival time. Response time equals the first time a job runs minus its arrival time. These metrics measure different things: early access to a processor does not necessarily imply early completion. First-come, first-served runs jobs in arrival order without preempting them. Shortest Job First selects the shortest available job and is non-preemptive. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Comparisons involving these shortest-job policies must state how execution lengths are known.

Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice before moving an unfinished job to the back. Shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but increase the frequency of context switches. Larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. Neither a smaller average response time nor a smaller switching fraction alone establishes that a policy is best for every objective.

A multi-level feedback queue, or MLFQ, uses observed execution behavior instead of requiring exact future job lengths. Jobs in higher-priority queues run before lower-priority jobs; equal-priority jobs can share service by Round Robin. New jobs begin at high priority, and consuming the allowed CPU allotment causes demotion. Accounting for total consumed allotment prevents a job from retaining high priority indefinitely merely by yielding just before each slice ends. Periodic priority boosts can help jobs otherwise left waiting at low priority. Queue levels, slice lengths, allotments, and boost intervals are policy parameters, not universal constants.

This fixture adds an explicit scheduling model for exercises. It is authored example scaffolding rather than text copied from a textbook. Unless a question states otherwise, there is one processor, jobs are independent, and each job consists of one CPU burst with no I/O. Arrival times and required CPU service are provided. The processor never serves two jobs simultaneously. Time spent switching is not CPU service delivered to any job. A job that finishes before its slice ends does not use the remaining slice. If a job arrives at exactly a slice boundary, the question must say whether that arrival is enqueued before or after the preempted job. Ties must be resolved by an explicit rule, such as alphabetical job names.

A question that includes switching overhead must define when that overhead applies: for example, only when moving between different jobs, with no initial dispatch charge. It must also state whether arrivals can occur while switching and how they enter the queue. Questions that ignore overhead must say so. These conventions make a timeline reproducible and prevent a numeric answer from depending on unstated simulator behavior.

A comparison can report each job's first-run and completion times, then compute the requested averages. A design recommendation also needs an objective and constraints, such as a maximum response time, a switching budget, or a fairness requirement. A policy can satisfy one constraint while losing on another metric. Choosing a scheduler should therefore follow the stated workload and requirements. response.evidence_note: All conventions needed for a reproducible timeline (one processor, single CPU bursts, slice-boundary arrival ordering, switch-cost timing, tie-breaking by name) are stated in the fixture and can be verified with cpu_schedule_v1.
learning_objectives: Apply Round Robin with an explicit switch-cost model to build a per-job first-run and completion timeline.
Distinguish response time from turnaround time and compute both.

sections.heading: Scheduling Metrics and Policy Conventions
sections.text: Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time; response time = first run time − arrival time. In Round Robin, a selected job runs at most one time slice, then an unfinished job returns to the back of the ready queue. Smaller slices can improve initial responsiveness but raise context-switch frequency; larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. For a reproducible timeline we fix: one processor, independent single-burst jobs, no I/O; arrivals during a switch enter the queue at the tail; an arrival exactly at a slice boundary is enqueued before the unfinished job is requeued; ties are broken by lexicographic job name; initial dispatch and dispatch after an idle interval are free; a switch cost applies only between different jobs, and if the previous job finished early (in less than a full slice) the next different-job switch is free. STCF is preemptive and picks the least remaining time (tie: lexicographic name).

questions.stem:
Consider Round Robin on one processor with jobs A (arrival 0, burst 7), B (arrival 2, burst 4), C (arrival 9, burst 1), and D (arrival 12, burst 2). One time unit is spent switching courses whenever the processor moves between two different jobs; switching adds no service to any job. Additional conventions: initial dispatch is free; an arrival exactly at a slice boundary is enqueued before the unfinished job is requeued; arrivals during a switch enter the queue at the tail; ties use lexicographic job name; early-finish free applies (if the previous job completed in less than a full slice, the next different-job switch costs 0).

(a) Build the full timeline for slice q = 3 (who runs when, including switch intervals) and give each job's first-run time and completion time.
(b) Compute each job's response time and turnaround time, and the two averages.
(c) Redo (a)–(b) with q = 1, but only report each job's first-run time and completion time, plus the average response time and average turnaround time. Then state the total number of time units spent switching for q = 3 and for q = 1, and answer: under a requirement that total switching time must not exceed 3 units, is q = 1 or q = 3 acceptable? Explain using the tradeoff between initial responsiveness and switching frequency.
questions.answer:
(a) q = 3 timeline (time is labeled by the interval [start, end); switch intervals are shown as 'switch'): [0,3) A; [3,6) B; [6,7) A; [7,8) switch; [8,10) B; [10,11) switch; [11,14) A; [14,15) switch; [15,16) D; [16,17) switch; [17,18) C. First-run / completion: A 0 / 14; B 3 / 10; C 17 / 18; D 15 / 16. Response times: A 0, B 1, C 8, D 3; average 3. Turnaround times: A 14, B 8, C 9, D 4; average 8.75.
(b) q = 1 timeline: [0,1) A; [1,2) switch; [2,3) B; [3,4) switch; [4,5) A; [5,6) switch; [6,7) B; [7,8) switch; [8,9) A; [9,10) switch; [10,11) B; [11,12) switch; [12,13) A; [13,14) switch; [14,15) A; [15,16) switch; [16,17) D; [17,18) switch; [18,19) C. First-run / completion: A 0 / 15; B 2 / 11; C 18 / 19; D 16 / 17. Response times: A 0, B 0, C 9, D 4; average 3.25. Turnaround times: A 15, B 9, C 10, D 5; average 9.75. Switching time: q = 3 uses 5 units; q = 1 uses 6 units. Under the ≤ 3-unit switching budget, neither q = 1 nor q = 3 is acceptable. The example illustrates the tradeoff: q = 1 slightly changes average response time but spends more time switching than q = 3, while neither slice respects the budget, so a policy must be chosen only after checking the stated objective and constraint.
questions.explanation: Round Robin rotates jobs, so a job's first run (response) and its completion (turnaround) depend on the queue and switching conventions stated in the question. With q = 3, A runs first, B next, and the unfinished jobs return to the back; switch costs occur between different-job transitions, except the switch after B finishes early (B completes after 2 units of its slice) is free. With q = 1, the same rotation occurs but switching occurs more often. Count each switch interval and add it to the timeline before computing completion times; then apply response = first run − arrival and turnaround = completion − arrival.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires constructing two reproducible RR timelines under a full set of stated conventions, tracking completion and first-run times, computing response and turnaround averages, and evaluating a switching budget: this integrates analysis, evaluation, and design judgment rather than recalling a definition.

expected_steps: Build the q = 3 timeline using queue rotation, boundary/tie/arrival conventions, and switch intervals (early-finish free switch after B completes).
Read first-run and completion times for each job, then calculate response and turnaround averages.
Build the q = 1 timeline under the same conventions and report first-run and completion times.
Compute average response and turnaround for q = 1 and total switching time for both slices.
Evaluate the two slices against the ≤ 3 switching budget and explain the response-time versus switching-frequency tradeoff.

sections.heading: Scheduling Model and Metrics
sections.text: One processor, independent single-burst jobs, no I/O. Turnaround time = completion − arrival. Response time = first start − arrival. When switching overhead is charged, no CPU service is delivered during a switch. A job that finishes before its slice ends does not use the remainder; if it finished early, the next different-process switch is free. In this task, switching cost is 1 unit per different-process transition, and an early-finish transition costs 0. Arrivals at a slice boundary enter the ready queue before the just-preempted job is requeued. Round Robin runs each selected job for at most one quantum before an unfinished job goes to the back of the queue.
